items.title: Brain Predicts Spoken Mandarin Differently Than English
items.snippet: Most neuroscience models of how we predict upcoming speech are based on English and European languages. Researchers recorded brain activity during a Mandarin audiobook, revealing that Mandarin listeners rely on tone-integrated sub-syllables rather than individual phonemes to anticipate speech.

items.title: Adolescent Brain Circuits Shape Lifelong Social Drive
items.snippet: Why are teenagers hard-wired to seek peer connection, and why do so many psychiatric disorders emerge during adolescence? Researchers found that disrupting a key prefrontal-to-striatum reward circuit during adolescence causes lasting social withdrawal in adulthood.

items.title: Why Nerve Pain Lingers
items.snippet: Why can a light touch trigger intense discomfort long after a nerve injury heals? Researchers uncovered a Nono–Kcnq2 molecular pathway in the spinal cord that normally brakes pain-neuron firing, and showed that restoring it relieves neuropathic pain.

items.title: Rising Blood Sugar in Young Adults Hurts Midlife Brain Health
items.snippet: Gradually rising blood sugar starting in your 20s can quietly erode cognitive performance decades before old age. A 30-year study found that young adults with creeping glucose levels scored worse on midlife memory and executive function tests, even without developing Type 2 diabetes.

items.title: Stanford scientists discover 3 hidden brain types behind ADHD and anxiety
items.snippet: An AI-powered analysis of thousands of children's brain scans has revealed three distinct brain types underlying ADHD and anxiety that do not neatly fit traditional diagnoses. These hidden biological patterns can appear before a diagnosis is made, potentially enabling earlier detection and more effective, personalized treatments.

items.title: What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach
items.snippet: A new theory suggests that the brain may chemically encode and retrieve memories rather than relying solely on electrical signals. Researchers propose that interactions between brain cells and their molecular surroundings could help explain the intimate connection between memory, emotion, and thought.
